Its range spans the middle and upper register, with a clear grain to each note and well-defined intervals. The hollow tube inside resonates naturally, giving the sound a distinctive colour somewhere between the yangqin and the guzheng. The Malagasy tube zither (valiha) is the tube zither of Madagascar, regarded as the national instrument, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 312.11. It is made from local bamboo; traditionally the strings are cut from the bamboo itself and raised and tuned on small gourd or wooden bridges, while today bicycle brake cable run through nails is often used, and serious players may change to guitar or piano strings. The bamboo tube is 5 to 10 cm across and 35 to 180 cm long, usually with 21 to 24 strings. It is plucked with the long fingernails, and the Malagasy prized it especially under Merina rule, using it for entertainment and for ritual music that summons spirits.
馬達加斯加管狀齊特琴（Valiha）為弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs: The Malagasy tube zither (valiha) is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 312.11, regarded as the national instrument of Madagascar. Local origin stories say it came from King David, which ties in with accounts of the Jewish origin of the Malagasy. It was historically made of bamboo, and modern instruments use a species with longer internodes; early strings were raised from the bamboo itself, while bicycle brake cable, guitar strings and piano strings are common now. It was valued under Merina rule, where playing with the long fingernails was a mark of nobility, and it is also used in rituals that summon spirits. The marovany variant is box-shaped and made of wood or metal. Rakotozafy's recordings (he was born in 1938) were mostly made live at Malagasy radio.
